title: Who's On First Neighbourhoods, Macrohoods and Microhoods
description:
**Level 5 of this catalog's administrative ladder: `macrohood`, `neighbourhood`, `microhood`.** Neighbourhoods, the macrohoods that bundle them and the microhoods inside them. "One thing is certain — neighbourhoods are things no one will completely agree on. Ever."

397,416 features from Who's On First, the open gazetteer, as geocode.earth's combined admin distribution publishes it. This is place-name and boundary lookup, not address geocoding: there is no street or house number anywhere in Who's On First's admin distribution.

The GeoParquet here is **this catalog's own optimized copy**: the same 397,416 features, sorted by `(country, wof_id)` with the sort declared, in 98 exactly-full row groups of 4096 (1.0 MiB each), zstd compressed, with a Parquet page index and a GeoParquet 1.1 `covering` bbox. geocode.earth's combined file is the right thing to read for a scan, an export or a spatial query, and this collection links straight to it. It is the wrong thing to read for **one** place: it has 83 row groups of 65,536 rows, no declared sort, and 89% of its bytes in the geometry column, so one row group's geometry chunk is a median of 38 MiB and as much as 285 MiB — which is what any row-group-granular reader, including the hyparquet a browser uses, pays to decode a single row. Filtering to one placetype prunes nothing either, because `placetype` statistics span most of the alphabet in most row groups.

Both files are assets of this collection, and the asset descriptions say which to use when. The [agent guide](AGENTS.md) has the join keys, the traps and queries that run.

**The license is a mix, and this catalog does not pretend otherwise.** Who's On First scopes CC0 to "the format and structure that allows Who's On First to operate" and the records inherit terms from over 300 sources, so the `license` field is `other` with links to [the per-source list](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/licenses/). Measured on this distribution's own `geom_src` column, 70.88% of the geometry is GeoNames under CC BY, 2.58% is CC0, and 14 records out of 5,423,663 are share-alike. Attribution is required: *Data from Who's On First. [License](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/licenses/).*

providers.name: Who's On First
providers.description: Produces the gazetteer. A community project, originally from Mapzen, that assembles place records from over 300 open data sources with a stable numeric identifier, a placetype hierarchy and names in hundreds of languages, and publishes the per-record geometry provenance that makes its licensing checkable.

providers.name: geocode.earth
providers.description: Builds and hosts the distributions. Who's On First lives as 260 GitHub repositories of GeoJSON; geocode.earth compiles them into combined GeoParquet, SQLite, SpatiaLite, GeoJSON-bundle and PMTiles files and serves them over HTTPS with range requests and permissive CORS, which is what makes this a metadata-first catalog rather than a copy. whosonfirst.org's own download page points here. (The Portolan `host` role names the organization serving *this catalog's* files, so it sits on Portolan Mirrors; geocode.earth hosts the upstream assets linked from every collection.)

providers.name: Portolan Mirrors
providers.description: Describes geocode.earth's distribution as a Portolan catalog and adds the three things a browser client cannot get from it: one GeoParquet per administrative level with small row groups, a display-simplified companion for the polygon-heavy levels, and a name index sorted for prefix search. Links to the upstream files rather than copying them wherever they already do the job. Adds no places and changes no attribute value.

table:columns.name: wof_id
table:columns.description: Attested. The Who's On First identifier, and the key everything in this catalog joins on. WOF documents `wof:id` as "The record's unique numeric integer identifier that are typically derived from Brooklyn Integers" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/)). It is published here as a decimal string rather than an integer so that this file, the gazetteer index and `parent_id` all join without a cast; upstream it is an INT32.

table:columns.name: parent_id
table:columns.description: Attested. The `wof_id` of the direct parent record, as a string. WOF reserves four negative values, and **they are not ids**: `-1` "unknown parent, record needs review", `-2` "shrug, this feature is complicated", `-3` "contested, but not disputed.. used for placetypes below the locality level", `-4` "multiple 'legal' parents.. used for placetypes at the locality level or above" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/)). This build maps `-1` to null; the other three are carried through, so a join on `parent_id` has to exclude them.

table:columns.name: name
table:columns.description: Attested. The display name. WOF documents `wof:name` as "An English UTF-7 transliterated representation of the name" — the encoding name is a typo in WOF's own documentation for UTF-8, and the values are UTF-8. Its names documentation is the useful statement: "`wof:name` is English by default and is a string (rather than a list of strings) that can be used for labels" ([wof names](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/names/)). Every other language lives in the `names` collection, one row per spelling.

table:columns.name: placetype
table:columns.description: Attested. The WOF placetype, which is what WOF has instead of an administrative level. The canonical list, each one's role and its permitted parents are in [whosonfirst-placetypes](https://github.com/whosonfirst/whosonfirst-placetypes); the project's own website page for them is out of date. WOF's definitions are blunt and worth reading: a `region` holds "places that would have a bone in a 'states rights' argument", a `locality` is "Towns and cities, independent of size or population. Things with neighbourhoods, basically", a `borough` is "A local government unit, below the `locality` placetype. Think Brooklyn".

table:columns.name: level
table:columns.description: Derived. This catalog's mapping of `placetype` onto the 0-based administrative ladder a name search needs: 0 country, dependency and disputed; 1 macroregion and region; 2 macrocounty and county; 3 localadmin; 4 locality and borough; 5 macrohood, neighbourhood and microhood. **Who's On First publishes no such number.** A level here is a tier, and a tier can hold a unit and its own subdivision, because WOF inserts `macroregion` above `region` and `microhood` below `neighbourhood` without adding a rung anyone else recognizes. The mapping is defined once, in `PLACETYPE_LEVEL` in `tools/wofcommon.py`.

table:columns.name: country
table:columns.description: Derived. ISO 3166-1 alpha-3, mapped from WOF's own two-letter code through the official ISO 3166-1 table packaged with pycountry, so this catalog and its two sibling gazetteer catalogs can be filtered with one code system. WOF's six synthetic codes have no alpha-3 and are carried through unchanged: see `country_iso2`.

table:columns.name: country_iso2
table:columns.description: Attested. WOF's own code, byte for byte. Documented as "A two-letter country code from ISO 3166" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/)), with six codes WOF mints itself and ISO does not have ([whosonfirst-placetypes](https://github.com/whosonfirst/whosonfirst-placetypes)): `XK` Kosovo ("We just followed Geonames' lead"), `XN` Null Island, `XS` Somaliland, `XX` "a place disputed by two or more (ISO) countries", `XY` "an ISO country that has yet to be determined (by us)", `XZ` "the ISO country code equivalent of `wof:parent_id=-2`".

table:columns.name: placetype_local
table:columns.description: Attested. "What locals consider the placetype to be (string value)" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/), `wof:placetype_local`). Free text and in the local language or English depending on the record: `district`, `voivodeship`, `département`. Useful for a label, not for a filter.

table:columns.name: repo
table:columns.description: Attested. The `whosonfirst-data-admin-{cc}` GitHub repository this record comes from. geocode.earth's combined distribution is the union of 260 of them, and this column is what says which. The members of the build are listed in its sidecar manifest, `whosonfirst-data-admin-latest.parquet.json`.

table:columns.name: lat
table:columns.description: Attested. "The latitude of a feature's geometric centroid" ([geom properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/geom/), `geom:latitude`). It is a centroid, so for a concave or multipart feature it can fall outside the feature. WOF publishes a separate hand-placed label point under `lbl:latitude`, which geocode.earth's parquet build does not carry.

table:columns.name: lon
table:columns.description: Attested. "The longitude of a feature's geometric centroid" ([geom properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/geom/), `geom:longitude`). See `lat`.

table:columns.name: min_zoom
table:columns.description: Attested. WOF's own answer to how early a place should appear on a map. `mz:min_zoom` and `mz:max_zoom` are "Float values (though in practice mosts are integer values) that match to web map zoom schema. Common range is 0.0 to 18.0, though they can be greater" ([mz properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/mz/)). For a gazetteer this is a better prominence signal than area, and no other catalog in this family has it.

table:columns.name: max_zoom
table:columns.description: Attested. The upper end of the same pair. See `min_zoom`.

table:columns.name: min_label
table:columns.description: Researched. The zoom at which a label for this place should first be drawn. **WOF publishes no definition for `mz:min_label` or `mz:max_label`** — neither appears on the [mz properties page](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/mz/), which documents `min_zoom` and `max_zoom` only. Pelias reads the pair for label placement, and the values here sit slightly above the matching `min_zoom`, which is consistent with "draw the shape at min_zoom, the label at min_label". Treat the meaning as inferred rather than stated.

table:columns.name: max_label
table:columns.description: Researched. The upper end of the same undocumented pair. See `min_label`.

table:columns.name: population
table:columns.description: Attested. "An integer value to represent the most current, known population of a place" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/), `wof:population`). Present only where a source supplied one, which is a minority of records at every level; the per-level coverage is in this collection's README. WOF also publishes `wof:population_rank` on a 0-to-14 band scale, which geocode.earth's parquet build does not carry.

table:columns.name: is_funky
table:columns.description: Attested. WOF's own "needs a human" flag. `mz:is_funky`: "-1 is unknown, or TBD (needs the love and care of a human) / 0 is false / 1 is true" ([mz properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/mz/)). Almost always absent, so a null means "not flagged", not "fine".

table:columns.name: modified
table:columns.description: Attested. When the WOF record last changed. WOF stores `wof:lastmodified` as "A Unix epoch timestamp integer" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/)); geocode.earth's build converts it to a date. It is the record's date, not this distribution's: the GeoParquet build itself is from 2025-04-07.

table:columns.name: country_wof_id
table:columns.description: Researched. The `wof_id` of the country this record sits in, flattened out of WOF's `wof:hierarchy` ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/): "A list of hashes, where each object is the list of ancestors") by geocode.earth's parquet build. The full hierarchy, including records with several parents, is **not** in the GeoParquet; it is in the SQLite and GeoJSON distributions.

table:columns.name: region_wof_id
table:columns.description: Researched. The `wof_id` of the containing region, from the same flattened hierarchy. See `country_wof_id`.

table:columns.name: county_wof_id
table:columns.description: Researched. The `wof_id` of the containing county, from the same flattened hierarchy. See `country_wof_id`.

table:columns.name: iso_code
table:columns.description: Derived. An ISO 3166-2 subdivision code, such as `AL-01`. Measured: present on 4,082 of 4,362 level-1 features and almost nowhere else. It arrives from WOF's `iso:code` concordance, so it is the same value a `concordance_keys = 'iso:code'` row carries.

table:columns.name: hasc_id
table:columns.description: Researched. A Hierarchical Administrative Subdivision Code, such as `AR.CT`. One of the identifier systems WOF keeps concordances against ([concordances](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/concordances/)). Mostly populated at level 1.

table:columns.name: geonames_id
table:columns.description: Researched. The [GeoNames](https://www.geonames.org/) identifier for the same place, from WOF's `gn:id` concordance. This is the most useful column in the file for cross-referencing, because GeoNames is also where most of the geometry came from: 3,843,415 of this distribution's records carry `geom_src = 'geonames'`.

table:columns.name: wikidata_id
table:columns.description: Researched. The [Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/) Q-identifier, from WOF's `wd:id` concordance.

table:columns.name: concordance_keys
table:columns.description: Derived. **One** concordance key, not the set. WOF's `wof:concordances` is "A hash containing identifiers from other data sources" ([wof properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/wof/)) and a record often holds several; geocode.earth's parquet build flattens it to a single key/id pair beside the separate `gn_id`, `wd_id` and `hasc_id` columns. Measured at level 1: 30 distinct keys over 4,282 populated rows, led by `iso:code` (2,830), `qs:local_id` (491) and `os:census_code` (178). If you need the whole concordance set, read the SQLite or GeoJSON distribution instead.

table:columns.name: concordance_ids
table:columns.description: Derived. The identifier belonging to `concordance_keys`. See that column for why there is only one.

table:columns.name: geom_src
table:columns.description: Attested. **The provenance and licensing key, and the most important column here.** WOF documents `src:geom` as "The data source of a record's geometry. Valid property values are listed in the whosonfirst-sources repository" ([src properties](https://whosonfirst.org/docs/properties/src/)). Join it to [sources-spec-latest.json](https://github.com/whosonfirst/whosonfirst-sources) and a specific feature's license is a fact rather than an average. Measured over the whole distribution: `geonames` 3,843,415, `karmashapes` 866,821, `quattroshapes` 180,884, `qs_pg` 144,246, `frgov` 69,118, `mz` 51,832, `whosonfirst` 45,222, `uscensus` 36,472.

table:columns.name: area_km2
table:columns.description: Derived. Geodesic area in square kilometres, from pyproj's `Geod`, which is GeographicLib. **Not** from DuckDB's `ST_Area_Spheroid`, which returns NaN for a large minority of these geometries — 12,814 of 42,115 counties — including closed, simple, valid polygons with finite coordinates. Reproducible, not official: it is measured on the geometry in this file, which for a feature whose outline was carried up from a coarser source is not that place's surveyed area, and it measures land only, so a country comes out a little under its published figure. A point feature is 0.

table:columns.name: perimeter_km
table:columns.description: Derived. Geodesic perimeter in kilometres, from the same pyproj `Geod` call. Paired with `area_km2` it gives a compactness measure without reprojecting anything.

table:columns.name: vertices
table:columns.description: Derived. Coordinates in the geometry, from `ST_NPoints`. This is the number behind this catalog's display files: a median country is 4,866 coordinates and a median locality is 1. A value of 1 means the geometry is a point, not a polygon.

table:columns.name: geometry_repaired
table:columns.description: Derived. True where the upstream geometry failed `ST_IsValid` and this build rebuilt it with `ST_MakeValid` and `ST_CollectionExtract(..., 3)`. 480 of 5,405,294 features across the catalog: 29 regions, 74 counties, 44 local administrative units, 307 localities, 26 neighbourhoods. Every other geometry is written through unchanged. The repair exists because `ST_Intersection` against an invalid polygon raises `TopologyException` and takes the whole query with it; geocode.earth's own file is where to read the unrepaired shape.

table:columns.name: geometry_flattened
table:columns.description: Derived. True where the upstream geometry carried a Z coordinate and this build dropped it with `ST_Force2D`. Exactly two features in the whole distribution do: the Swiss counties Arbon (`wof_id` 102062959) and Neuchâtel (unincorporated) (`wof_id` 1394237543), whose Z values are elevations in metres. That is why the upstream file's GeoParquet metadata declares a six-element bbox with a `zmin` of 394.915 for the whole planet. A Z coordinate means nothing for an administrative boundary and mixing 2D and 3D in one column breaks readers — `gpq validate` rejects such a file with "wkb: unsupported geometry" — so every geometry here is 2D.

table:columns.name: bbox
table:columns.description: Derived. The feature's bounding box in EPSG:4326 degrees, as four doubles declared in the GeoParquet 1.1 `covering` metadata, so a reader can prune row groups spatially without decoding any geometry.

table:columns.name: geometry
table:columns.description: Attested. WKB, EPSG:4326 (OGC:CRS84), exactly the coordinates WOF publishes except for the 480 rows `geometry_repaired` flags and the 2 rows `geometry_flattened` flags. A point where `vertices = 1`, otherwise a Polygon or MultiPolygon, always 2D.
